Colorimetry and spectra — colour is fixed only by spectrum × illuminant × observer

fullseye does have colorimetry proper (the imgmetrics family: rgb_to_lab / delta_e_2000 and others). The 2-D colour ops (trans_from_rgb / trans_to_rgb / cfa_to_rgb / linear_trans_color and others), on the other hand, are colour-space conversions, not colorimetry. When visual inspection has to decide "the colour is different", looking only at RGB differences will miss somewhere, without fail. This document is not a description of ops; it is teaching material on the physics and conventions that come before them. It sits in the same position as optics/guides/mv_*.md (imaging chain), 3d/guides/depth_sensors.md (depth) and annotate/guides/dataset_conventions.md (output side).

1. The defining equation of colour (everything follows from here)

An object colour is not determined by the object alone. The tristimulus values are integrals of a product of 3 factors:

X = k ∫ S(λ) · R(λ) · x̄(λ) dλ
Y = k ∫ S(λ) · R(λ) · ȳ(λ) dλ
Z = k ∫ S(λ) · R(λ) · z̄(λ) dλ

S(λ) = spectral power distribution of the illuminant   R(λ) = spectral reflectance of the object   x̄ȳz̄ = colour-matching functions (observer)
k is normalised so that Y = 100 for a perfect diffuse reflector

Anything not in this equation cannot determine colour. In other words:

• Change the illuminant and the colour changes (even for the same object).

• Change the observer and the colour changes — the CIE 1931 2° standard observer and the CIE 1964 10° standard observer are different things. Inspection fields of view are wide, so there are situations where the 10° observer is used. Lab values that do not state which observer they were measured with cannot be compared.

• Camera RGB is not the output of this equation (§4).

2. Standard illuminants — the name and the substance disagree

| Symbol | Substance | Correlated colour temperature |

| --- | --- | --- |

| D65 | Average daylight (the D series was defined statistically from measurements in 1964) | about 6504 K |

| D50 | Reference for printing and graphic arts | about 5003 K |

| A | Tungsten lamp (blackbody) | 2856 K |

| F1–F12 | Fluorescent lamps (12 types) | Depends on the type |

The correlated colour temperature of D65 is not exactly 6500 K because the estimated value of the constant c₂ in Planck's law was revised after the standard was fixed. The name has stayed at 6500.

And what matters is this — neither the D series nor the F series can in practice be reproduced artificially to any real degree (they are mathematically defined distributions, not real light sources). Furthermore:

> LEDs fit neither the D series nor the F series.

Illumination for visual inspection is now almost entirely LED. That means looking up a table of standard illuminants will not give you the S(λ) on the shop floor. Measuring with a spectroradiometer, or using the manufacturer's spectral data, is the only reliable route.

3. Metamerism — the landmine most often stepped on in inspection

There exist pairs that have different spectral reflectances R(λ) yet whose tristimulus values match under a particular illuminant. Such a pair is called a metameric pair.

As long as you integrate first and compare afterwards, this cannot be avoided. The moment you reduce to 3 numbers (XYZ), the information in the infinite-dimensional R(λ) has been discarded. As a result:

• The verdict changes between day and night (happens in inspection booths where ambient light leaks in)

• Visual check OK, but camera NG (human colour-matching functions and camera sensitivity differ, §4)

• The pass rate changed after the lighting was replaced with LEDs from another lot (S(λ) differs slightly)

If you want to discriminate them, the only way is to measure spectrally. Neither RGB nor XYZ is enough. Conversely, when someone says "we control it by colour difference", unless which illuminant and which observer are fixed, that control will not reproduce.

4. A camera is not an observer

A real camera whose spectral sensitivities are a linear combination of the colour-matching functions (the Luther–Ives condition) practically does not exist. Therefore:

• A 3×3 matrix for RGB → XYZ / Lab is an approximation that holds only for that illuminant and that set of subjects. Take it to another illuminant or another set of materials and systematic errors appear (camera metamerism).

• That is why you calibrate with a colour chart. Shoot an X-Rite ColorChecker (24 patches) or similar under the same lighting and the same exposure, and estimate the transform by linear (or polynomial) regression against the known Lab of the patches. A ΔE computed from uncalibrated RGB is only a number.

Order of preprocessing (break it and colour breaks)

1. Dark current / offset subtraction

2. Shading (flat-field) correction — removes illumination non-uniformity and the lens cos⁴ fall-off

3. White balance — von Kries-type diagonal scaling, or more accurately the Bradford CAT

4. Compute in linear space — this is the key point. Averaging, resizing or interpolating without removing the sRGB gamma makes things darker and muddier (averaging in a non-linear space has no physical meaning)

5. Re-apply gamma only for display

Saturated pixels are invalid as colour. Clipping even 1 channel rotates the hue. In inspection, keep a separate saturation mask and exclude those pixels from the colour-difference calculation.

5. Colour difference ΔE — which one to use

| Formula | Year | Properties |

| --- | --- | --- |

| ΔE*ab (CIE76) | 1976 | Euclidean distance in Lab. Simple to implement but not perceptually uniform (deviates especially at high chroma) |

| ΔE94 (CIE94) | 1994 | Adds weights for lightness, chroma and hue. A large improvement over CIE76 |

| ΔE00 (CIEDE2000) | 2001 | Adds a rotation term and a grey correction on top. The most refined, but the formula is complex |

As a research finding, it has been reported that the improvement from CIE76 → CIE94 is larger than the improvement from CIE94 → CIEDE2000. As for the contributions of the CIEDE2000 correction terms, taking the chroma-difference correction as 100, the order is hue difference 29, rotation term 8, lightness difference 8, grey correction 6 — the chroma-difference correction dominates.

kL (the lightness weight) is changed by application — 1 for graphic arts and 2 for textiles is the convention. It is a value to be decided for the object under inspection, not something to be used as the default as is.

Treat "ΔE = 1 is the limit of discrimination" as folklore. The actual discrimination threshold changes with hue, chroma, lightness, background and viewing conditions. Measure the threshold on your own objects, under your own viewing conditions, and decide it from that.

6. Where fullseye stands now (honestly)

| Element | What exists now | What is missing |

| --- | --- | --- |

| Illuminant S(λ) | light_spec(source=led/halogen/laser, wavelength_nm, bandwidth_nm) — a centre wavelength + bandwidth model (with a catalogue of real illuminators) | Cannot hold a measured spectral distribution. No D65/A/F-series tables either |

| Reflectance R(λ) | scene_material(albedo=...) — scalar or RGB | Cannot hold spectral reflectance. So metamerism cannot be reproduced in principle |

| Observer x̄ȳz̄ | None | Colour-matching function tables for CIE 1931 2° / 1964 10° |

| Camera sensitivity | sensor_spec(qe=...) — scalar QE | QE(λ) curve, spectral transmittance of the colour filters |

| Colour-space conversion | imgmetrics's rgb_to_xyz / xyz_to_lab / rgb_to_lab / lab_to_rgb — by the CIE definitions, the white point is selectable with white= (default D65 2°) | White-point adaptation (Bradford CAT). The inverse transform clips out-of-gamut values, so a round trip matches only inside the gamut |

| Colour difference | delta_e_76 / delta_e_2000 / delta_e_map — CIEDE2000 is pinned by Sharma et al.'s 34 verification pairs (kL / kC / kH can be passed) | ΔE94. Spectrum-based colour difference |

How to use the metrics themselves (the data_range trap, implementation differences in SSIM, a template for attaching conditions to a report) is split out into imgmetrics/guides/image_difference_metrics.md.

★ The same conversion exists 3 times — same name, different scale

fullseye has RGB → L*a*b* 3 times:

| Where | Implementation | Scale / precision |

| --- | --- | --- |

| imgmetrics.rgb_to_lab | CIE definition (sRGB primaries, selectable white point) | float, L* is 0–100. This is the correct one |

| color_pca.trans_from_rgb(img, "lab") | Delegates to the above | Same values |

| trans_from_rgb in the op registry (backends_color) | OpenCV | 8-bit scale: quantised to uint8 before conversion, then divided by 255 |

An inconsistency found while writing this document was exactly this — color_pca.trans_from_rgb() accepted only hsv / yuv / gray, and passing "lab" or "xyz" raised ValueError. The correct implementation already existed in imgmetrics, but there was no path from the colour-space conversion entry point to reach it.

The fix was not "write one more implementation" but delegation. Holding two sets of matrices and transfer functions means that when only one of them is fixed, a different colour comes out without any exception (imgmetrics itself delegates the sRGB transfer function to gfx2d for the same reason).

Verification (tests/test_colorimetry.py): white → (100, 0, 0) (residual 2e-5 — because the published sRGB matrix is rounded to 7 digits), sRGB primaries → (53.241, 80.092, 67.203) and others match the published values, mid grey 0.5 → L* = 53.389 (not 50), and color_pca and imgmetrics return identical values.

7. Summary (the core of the judgement)

• If you manage colour by numbers, fix the illuminant, observer and white point first. A ΔE for which these are not fixed does not reproduce.

• An RGB difference is not a colour difference. It becomes a colour difference only after calibration with a colour chart.

• Do not try to separate things with different spectra using 3 numbers. That is metamerism, and it collapses the moment the lighting changes. If you want to separate them, measure spectrally.

• Compute in linear space. An average taken without removing gamma is not a physical quantity.

8. Diagnostic table — from symptom to cause

| Symptom | Suspect first | How to check |

| --- | --- | --- |

| Visual check OK, but camera NG | Camera spectral sensitivity differs from the human one (camera metamerism) | Measure the spectral reflectance. If that is impossible, shoot a calibration chart under the same conditions and see whether the residual is large in the neighbourhood of that colour |

| The verdict changes between day and night / with the season | Ambient light leaks in and S(λ) is changing | Check whether it reproduces with light blocked. Enclose with a blackout curtain and compare |

| The pass rate changed after the lighting was replaced | Spectral variation of LEDs (lot-to-lot differences exist even for the same model number) | Shoot the same reference plate with the old and new lighting and compare the channel ratios |

| The colour changed after shrinking or averaging the image | The computation was done in gamma space | Convert back to linear, apply the same processing and compare |

| The hue rotates only in bright areas | Saturation (clipping even 1 channel rotates it) | Look at the distribution of the per-channel maxima. Count the pixels stuck at the saturation value |

| The colour differs only at the edges of the field | Shading not corrected / peripheral illumination fall-off (cos⁴) | Shoot a white plate over the full field, take a flat field, then judge again |

| The ΔE numbers do not match the feel on the shop floor | Choice of formula (still CIE76) and kL | Switch to ΔE94 / ΔE00 and look at the correlation with the visual ranking. Re-decide the threshold by your own discrimination experiment |

| Lab values do not match another company's | Different white point and observer (D65/D50, 2°/10°) | Confirm the white point and observer with the other party. If they are not stated, do not compare |
